paragraphs: Image denoisers trained on large datasets can struggle when a new image differs from their training examples. Training a model on one noisy image offers adaptation, but provides little information to learn from. GainTuning combines these approaches by adjusting an already trained convolutional network to each individual test image.

The adjustment is deliberately restricted: the method learns one multiplicative gain for each channel in the network’s convolutional layers. These gains change how strongly existing channels contribute. Restricting adaptation to this small set of parameters is intended to avoid overfitting while retaining the knowledge acquired during large-scale training.

The authors report improvements on standard denoising benchmarks for nearly every image in a held-out test set. Gains are larger when test images systematically differ in noise level or image type. They also adapt a model trained on synthetic data to transmission electron microscope images. In that application, GainTuning faithfully reconstructs catalytic nanoparticle structure at extremely low signal-to-noise ratios, illustrating how selective adaptation can make pretrained denoisers useful under substantially different imaging conditions.
neurips-2021-adaptive-denoising-via-gain.tldr: GainTuning adapts pretrained image denoisers through per-channel scaling, improving results especially when test images differ from training data.

paragraphs: A neural network’s Hessian describes how the loss curves as its parameters change, including interactions between parameters. Its rank indicates how many independent directions this second-order description captures. The paper asks why this rank can be much smaller than the number of parameters, connecting that deficiency to the network’s structure.

The authors develop theoretical tools for analyzing the range of the Hessian map. For deep linear networks, these tools yield exact rank formulas and tight upper bounds. This gives a structural explanation for rank deficiency, extending beyond empirical low-rank approximations that do not explicitly account for how the network is constructed.

The work also examines how width, depth, and bias affect the deficiency. For broader model families, including rectified and hyperbolic tangent networks, the authors demonstrate that their bounds remain useful estimates of numerical Hessian rank. The distinction matters: exact formulas are established for deep linear networks, while the nonlinear results support the estimates’ wider relevance. Together, the findings clarify sources and extent of redundancy in overparameterized models.
neurips-2021-analytic-insights-into-stru.tldr: The paper explains structural causes of low Hessian rank, deriving exact results for deep linear networks and useful estimates for nonlinear models.

paragraphs: Accurate predictions do not automatically come with reliable confidence scores. This paper finds that the graph neural networks studied are primarily underconfident, contrasting with the overconfidence reported for many other neural networks. It addresses how to adjust those scores so that they better reflect the reliability of node predictions.

The authors observe that confidence has a homophily pattern in graphs: connected nodes tend to exhibit similar confidence. They use this finding to build CaGCN, a graph neural network that performs calibration after prediction. It uses graph topology to learn a node-specific transformation from the original prediction scores to calibrated confidence.

The transformation preserves the ordering of classes, so calibration retains the original predicted class and its accuracy. The authors also incorporate CaGCN into self-training, where model predictions become training labels. Calibrated confidence produces more trustworthy pseudo labels and improves performance in that setting. Experiments support benefits for calibration and accuracy, with accuracy preservation applying to the calibration transformation itself and further accuracy gains arising through its use in self-training.
neurips-2021-be-confident-towards-trustw.tldr: CaGCN uses graph structure to calibrate node confidence while preserving class rankings and improving pseudo labels for self-training.

paragraphs: The paper studies perception as two linked processes: external stimuli are encoded into internal signals, and a decoder turns those signals into an estimate. It derives approximations for the bias and variance of a Bayesian-mean decoder, assuming independent encoding signals that need not share the same distribution. Simulations support the approximations in the small-noise regime.

The analysis separates bias into a component associated with prior expectations and another associated with encoding precision. Under efficient encoding, these components push in opposite directions. Their relative strength depends on the objective being optimized, so adapting perception to different tasks can change the direction of its systematic errors.

This provides a unified explanation for biases both toward and away from prior expectations, without requiring an inconsistent account of optimal encoding and decoding. The authors also recover a relationship between bias and the derivative of variance, showing that its proportionality coefficient depends on the task. The contribution is a constrained optimal-perception theory in which both prior knowledge and task demands shape the observer’s responses.
neurips-2021-bias-and-variance-of-the-ba.tldr: Task-dependent encoding can explain why an optimal Bayesian-mean decoder produces biases either toward or away from prior expectations.

paragraphs: Aligning two point clouds requires identifying points that correspond across the two observations. Methods that first detect sparse keypoints can struggle when those detections are not repeatable. CoFiNet addresses this problem by constructing correspondences through a coarse-to-fine process that does not require keypoint detection.

At the coarse stage, the network matches downsampled nodes using a weighting scheme that favors neighborhoods with greater overlap. These matches narrow the search for detailed correspondences. The proposed nodes are then expanded into patches containing points and their descriptors. A density-adaptive matching module refines correspondences within overlapping patch regions, accommodating differences in point density.

Evaluations on indoor and outdoor benchmarks show advantages over existing approaches. On the low-overlap 3DLoMatch benchmark, the authors report at least a 5% improvement in Registration Recall over state-of-the-art methods while using at most two-thirds as many parameters. The findings support the value of first locating promising shared regions and then resolving their detailed matches, particularly when only a limited portion of the two point clouds overlaps.
neurips-2021-cofinet-reliable-coarse-to-.tldr: CoFiNet finds point-cloud correspondences through coarse-to-fine matching, improving registration especially when the clouds have little overlap.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to identify the best feasible collection of uncertain options when the collection’s value is determined by its weakest member. A learner samples individual base arms, but must ultimately choose a valid subset, called a super arm. Its bottleneck value is the smallest expected reward among its members.

The authors develop methods for two settings. With fixed confidence, the learner seeks a reliable answer using as few samples as possible. With a fixed budget, it must make the best identification possible from a prescribed number of samples. The bottleneck objective requires techniques beyond those used for the additive rewards common in earlier combinatorial exploration work.

For fixed confidence, the algorithms achieve optimal sample complexity within a logarithmic factor for a broad family of instances, supported by a matching lower bound. For fixed budget, the paper establishes a state-of-the-art error guarantee and efficient operation on path instances. Experiments involving top-k selection, paths, and matchings support advantages over the tested baselines, illustrating the benefit of exploiting the weakest-member structure directly.
neurips-2021-combinatorial-pure-explorat.tldr: The paper develops sample-efficient algorithms for finding constrained subsets whose weakest member has the highest expected reward.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows connect observations to a simple latent distribution through invertible transformations. This structure makes likelihood evaluation and sampling attractive, but the requirement of invertibility restricts model width and can limit expressive capacity. DenseFlow addresses that restriction by progressively adding noise to intermediate representations.

The added noise is preconditioned using earlier invertible units, creating what the authors call cross-unit coupling. Within each invertible module, the architecture combines a densely connected block with Nyström self-attention. Dense connections therefore operate both across units and inside modules, giving the model additional ways to combine information as representations pass through the flow.

These changes target the capacity of the transformations used for density modeling. The experiments report significant improvements from the proposed components and state-of-the-art density estimation under moderate computing budgets. The result supports the combination of incremental noise padding and dense coupling as a practical way to strengthen flow models. Its significance lies in improving the flexibility of this structured model family without making a claim that every flow architecture needs the same modifications.
neurips-2021-densely-connected-normalizi.tldr: DenseFlow expands intermediate representations with conditioned noise and dense connections to improve flow-based density estimation.

paragraphs: Training deep networks requires memory for intermediate activations. Two established ways to reduce that demand make different tradeoffs: rematerialization recomputes values when needed, while offloading moves them out of the constrained memory. This paper investigates how to coordinate both strategies so that computation and data movement can jointly reduce memory use.

The authors model the costs and constraints associated with frameworks such as PyTorch and TensorFlow. They then propose optimal algorithms for finding valid sequences of operations under memory constraints. The scheduling problem matters because decisions about retaining, moving, and recomputing activations interact; combining the strategies requires accounting for those interactions.

Experiments on realistic networks and computing platforms show that allowing offloading can eliminate one-third of rematerialization’s overhead. Together, the strategies reduce activation memory by a factor of four to six with overhead below 20% in the reported experiments. These results indicate that carefully coordinated memory management can make larger models, batches, or higher-resolution inputs more feasible, while keeping the additional training cost relatively modest in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-efficient-combination-of-re.tldr: Jointly scheduling activation recomputation and offloading substantially reduces training memory with limited overhead in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Visual transformers can represent global relationships within images, but they must learn some local visual properties that convolutional networks build into their architecture. This can make training data particularly important. The paper compares visual transformers under limited-data conditions and finds that similar ImageNet accuracy can conceal large differences on smaller datasets.

To improve training in this regime, the authors introduce an auxiliary self-supervised task that encourages learning spatial relationships within each image. It is optimized alongside the usual supervised objective, extracting additional training information from the images already available. The task adds negligible computational overhead and does not depend on a particular transformer architecture.

Experiments across multiple visual transformers and datasets show improved final accuracy, sometimes by a substantial amount, and greater robustness when training examples are scarce. The contribution therefore concerns both evaluation and training: success on a large dataset does not establish comparable behavior with less data, and an additional spatial learning objective can help existing transformers use small datasets more effectively without requiring an architecture-specific redesign.
neurips-2021-efficient-training-of-visua.tldr: An auxiliary spatial self-supervised task helps visual transformers learn more effectively from small datasets with negligible computational overhead.

paragraphs: Estimating the effect of changing several variables together is harder than estimating a single intervention. Each combination defines a different treatment group, creating many groups with limited observations. Confounding must also be addressed across those combinations, while each observed case reveals only its factual outcome rather than the alternatives.

Single-cause Perturbation tackles this problem in two stages. It first estimates outcomes under interventions that change one cause at a time and uses those estimates to augment the observational dataset. It then performs covariate adjustment on that augmented dataset to estimate effects involving multiple causes. Neither stage is tied to one particular estimation algorithm.

The authors formally establish the procedure’s validity under standard causal-inference assumptions and demonstrate performance gains in synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments. The assumption-dependent guarantee matters because the added outcomes are estimates, not newly observed interventions. The contribution is a flexible route from simpler single-cause estimation to a more complex multi-cause problem, using augmentation and adjustment together to address the scarcity of observations across treatment combinations.
neurips-2021-estimating-multi-cause-trea.tldr: Single-cause Perturbation combines estimated single-intervention outcomes with covariate adjustment to estimate multi-cause treatment effects under causal assumptions.

paragraphs: In a standard bandit problem, a learner explores uncertain options to discover which produces the best reward. This paper considers multiple agents who receive potentially different rewards from the same chosen option. An arm that is attractive to one agent may therefore be unattractive to another, making a single shared ranking inappropriate.

The goal becomes learning a fair probability distribution over arms. The authors formalize fairness through Nash social welfare and evaluate learning by the welfare lost while rewards are still being discovered. This places the distribution of benefits across agents directly inside the learning objective, rather than treating fairness as a separate assessment after choosing an arm.

The paper adapts three classical bandit algorithms to this multi-agent setting and proves sublinear regret measured in lost Nash social welfare. Consequently, average welfare regret per decision decreases as the interaction grows. An extension of a classical lower bound establishes optimality for one of the algorithms. Together, these results show that uncertainty about rewards can be handled with formal learning guarantees while pursuing the specified collective fairness objective.
neurips-2021-fair-algorithms-for-multi-a.tldr: The paper develops bandit algorithms that learn fair distributions over shared options using Nash social welfare, with sublinear regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Disease progression models must describe both a shared pattern over time and differences between patients. Geometric approaches represent patient trajectories around a central geodesic, a path determined by the geometry of the data space. They offer interpretable trajectory parameters, but choosing the metric in advance constrains the shapes those trajectories can take.

This paper learns that metric from longitudinal data while retaining the interpretable trajectory model. It constructs the metric by transporting Euclidean geometry through a diffeomorphism, a smooth invertible transformation. The transformation is estimated iteratively through compositions of radial basis functions, allowing the geometry itself to adapt to observed progression patterns.

Learning the metric improves forecasts of imaging and clinical biomarkers in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohort. The authors report results that compare favorably with the 56 methods benchmarked in the TADPOLE challenge. The contribution is therefore a more flexible geometric progression model: patient variation remains described through interpretable parameters, while the underlying trajectory shapes are informed by data rather than fixed entirely by a prior metric choice.
neurips-2021-learning-riemannian-metric-.tldr: Learning the geometry underlying patient trajectories improves disease-progression forecasts while preserving an interpretable trajectory model.

paragraphs: Neural representations can contain many numerical values, making compact binary alternatives appealing. The challenge is preserving useful information when compressing them into very short bit sequences. LLC learns binary codes for both individual examples and classes without requiring extra information such as annotated attributes or label metadata.

For ImageNet-1K, the method learns codes of approximately 20 bits while retaining nearly optimal classification accuracy for ResNet50. The learned codes also reveal an intuitive taxonomy among classes. This suggests that their compactness does not simply discard all relationships between categories: the representations retain structure that is meaningful for organizing the data.

The authors test the same representations for retrieval and out-of-distribution detection. On ImageNet-100 retrieval, 10-bit codes outperform 16-bit HashNet codes and match the accuracy of 10-dimensional real-valued representations. For out-of-distribution detection, they match a baseline that requires approximately 3,000 samples for threshold tuning, without using any such tuning samples. These findings support the usefulness of the learned binary representation across several tasks, beyond its original classification role.
neurips-2021-llc-accurate-multi-purpose-.tldr: LLC learns very short binary representations that retain strong classification, retrieval, and out-of-distribution detection performance without extra semantic metadata.

paragraphs: Filling missing entries in a dataset changes the relationships represented by that data. MIRACLE starts from the premise that these replacements should respect the causal structure of the process that generated the observations. Its goal is to improve imputation by considering both the values being filled and the mechanism responsible for their absence.

The method begins with the output of a baseline imputation approach and repeatedly refines it. During refinement, it also models how missingness is generated. A regularization scheme encourages the completed data to remain consistent with the underlying causal mechanism, allowing causal information to guide corrections to an existing imputation.

Experiments on synthetic and publicly available datasets report consistent improvements over a variety of benchmark methods. The evaluations cover data missing completely at random, at random, and not at random. These results support using the missingness mechanism as part of the imputation process across the tested settings. The method encourages causal consistency; the reported evidence establishes empirical improvements rather than an unconditional guarantee that every completed dataset recovers its true causal structure.
neurips-2021-miracle-causally-aware-impu.tldr: MIRACLE refines existing imputations by modeling missingness and encouraging consistency with the data’s causal structure.

paragraphs: Logged decisions can help evaluate a prospective policy when new experiments are unavailable. Much off-policy evaluation focuses on average reward, but an average does not capture every concern about outcomes. This paper develops a framework for assessing a broader range of risks, including variance, mean-variance objectives, and conditional value-at-risk.

Off-Policy Risk Assessment first estimates the target policy’s cumulative reward distribution, which describes the probability of outcomes below each threshold. It then substitutes that estimated distribution into the desired risk calculations. The authors define a class of Lipschitz risk functionals, enabling one distribution estimate to support a collection of different risk measures.

The framework is instantiated with importance-sampling and doubly robust estimators. The theoretical results provide uniform concentration guarantees for both distribution estimators and finite-sample risk bounds that hold simultaneously across the stated class. The risk estimation errors converge at order one over the square root of the sample count. This makes distribution estimation a reusable foundation for evaluating multiple aspects of policy risk, with shared statistical guarantees rather than separate analyses for each objective.
neurips-2021-off-policy-risk-assessment-.tldr: OPRA estimates a policy’s reward distribution from logged data and uses it to assess many risk measures with simultaneous finite-sample guarantees.

paragraphs: Estimating a matrix’s trace through matrix-vector products avoids needing direct access to every matrix entry. For positive-semidefinite matrices, the challenge is obtaining a relative-error guarantee using few queries and a small failure probability. This paper focuses on non-adaptive methods, whose queries do not depend on answers to earlier queries.

Non-adaptive methods support mergeable sketches, parallel computation, memory-efficient streaming, and distributed processing with low communication. The authors close a query-complexity gap between adaptive and non-adaptive approaches. Their method uses O(sqrt(log(1/delta))/epsilon + log(1/delta)) matrix-vector products, where epsilon controls relative error and delta controls failure probability.

They also prove lower bounds showing that the dependence on these two quantities cannot be improved by a non-adaptive algorithm beyond a log log(1/delta) factor. Thus, the theoretical result pairs an efficient construction with evidence of near-optimality. Experiments report superior performance over adaptive Hutch++, which offers less parallelism, and non-adaptive Hutchinson estimation. The work shows that high-probability trace estimation can retain the practical advantages of sketching without the previously known query penalty.
neurips-2021-optimal-sketching-for-trace.tldr: A non-adaptive trace estimator achieves near-optimal high-probability query complexity while retaining the parallel and streaming advantages of sketching.

paragraphs: High accuracy on ImageNet does not establish human-like robustness on unfamiliar images. This study compares human and machine vision across a broad collection of out-of-distribution datasets. It gathers 85,120 psychophysical trials from 90 participants and evaluates models differing in training objectives, architecture, and training-set size.

The results separate two questions: how often a system is correct and whether it makes mistakes on the same images as people. The strongest models exceed human feedforward performance on most tested out-of-distribution datasets, indicating progress on distortion robustness. Yet a substantial image-level consistency gap remains: people and models still tend to make different errors.

Models often agree with one another’s categorization mistakes even when their training approaches differ substantially. Increasing training-set size by one to three orders of magnitude improves human-model consistency in many cases. The findings therefore support cautious optimism about narrowing behavioral differences, while preserving the distinction between robust accuracy and human-like errors. The released benchmark combines 17 out-of-distribution datasets with image-level human responses and evaluation code to measure both aspects of future progress.
neurips-2021-partial-success-in-closing-.tldr: Leading vision models narrow the human robustness gap on tested datasets, but their image-level mistakes still differ substantially from people’s.

paragraphs: Particle-collision jets consist of correlated particles and can naturally be represented as sets of points in momentum space. Generative models could accelerate their simulation, but producing physically useful particle clouds requires more than adopting a generic point-cloud generator. This paper introduces the JetNet dataset to support that task.

The authors first apply existing point-cloud generative adversarial networks and find them inadequate for the physics application. They assess generated samples through feature-distribution comparisons, a newly developed Fréchet ParticleNet Distance, coverage, and minimum matching distance. They then develop MPGAN, a generative adversarial network based on message passing for particle-cloud generation.

MPGAN outperforms the tested point-cloud GANs on virtually every evaluation metric and shows promise for high-energy physics use. The paper also establishes it as a benchmark for subsequent models and releases a JetNet Python package with dataset interfaces, evaluation measures, and loss tools. The contribution combines a stronger generator with shared research infrastructure, while the stated findings indicate potential for simulation rather than claiming a completed replacement for existing physics simulation.
neurips-2021-particle-cloud-generation-w.tldr: MPGAN improves particle-cloud generation over tested point-cloud GANs, alongside a new JetNet dataset and evaluation toolkit.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning must distinguish target classes using very few labeled examples. POODLE adds another source of information: unlabeled examples from outside those classes. Such examples indicate what the classifier should separate from its target categories, helping it avoid features that are irrelevant to the current classification task.

The method adjusts class prototypes by increasing their distance from out-of-distribution examples while reducing their distance from in-distribution examples, including support and query data in the described approach. This creates complementary signals: target examples draw prototypes toward useful regions, while outside examples push them away from regions associated with irrelevant content.

POODLE is lightweight, does not add pretraining cost, and can work with different feature extractors. The authors describe its applicability to both inductive and transductive settings and report consistent improvements across standard benchmarks using pretrained networks with different architectures. The findings suggest that readily available examples outside the target classes can be a useful resource for few-shot adaptation, even though they do not supply additional labels for the classes being learned.
neurips-2021-poodle-improving-few-shot-l.tldr: POODLE improves few-shot classification by moving class prototypes away from unlabeled examples outside the target classes.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why starting gradient descent with small random parameter values can help overparameterized models learn useful solutions. Its concrete setting is low-rank matrix reconstruction from a limited set of measurements, expressed as a nonconvex optimization problem. The analysis links the early optimization steps to spectral learning.

The authors approximately divide the trajectory into three phases. First, the iterates develop a spectral bias that aligns their column space sufficiently with that of the underlying matrix. Next, they move away from certain degenerate saddle points. Finally, a local refinement phase brings rapid convergence to the target low-rank matrix.

The analysis shows that the implicit spectral bias is more prominent with overparameterization and guides optimization toward solutions that are globally optimal and generalize well in the studied setting. Small random initialization thus plays an active role in shaping the learning trajectory. The authors suggest that the analytical insights may extend to other computational problems, but the stated reconstruction guarantees concern the specific low-rank matrix formulation rather than arbitrary overparameterized neural networks.
neurips-2021-small-random-initialization.tldr: For low-rank matrix reconstruction, small random initialization induces spectral alignment that guides gradient descent toward accurate, generalizing solutions.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks offer attractive transfer and multitask properties for locomotion policies, but their performance has deteriorated as controlled agents gain more sensors and actuators. This creates a scaling problem: successful control of small agents does not automatically carry over to larger systems with more continuous control dimensions.

The paper attributes this degradation to increasingly unstable policy updates caused by overfitting in parts of the network. Snowflake addresses that mechanism by freezing parameters in selected network components during training. Restricting which parameters change is intended to curb the local overfitting responsible for unstable updates and improve learning on larger agents.

The authors report substantial gains in graph-based locomotion control for large agents. With Snowflake, graph neural networks match multilayer perceptron performance while retaining superior transfer properties. The result highlights training dynamics as a barrier to scaling these policies: changing which components are allowed to learn can improve performance without abandoning the graph-based representation. The stated evidence concerns locomotion control on the evaluated large agents, where both control performance and transfer are relevant.
neurips-2021-snowflake-scaling-gnns-to-h.tldr: Snowflake freezes selected GNN parameters to stabilize learning and improve locomotion control on agents with many sensors and actuators.

paragraphs: In games with hidden information, solving the current subgame often requires considering a common-knowledge closure: all situations that must remain in view given the players’ shared knowledge. This set can become impractically large. The paper instead uses low-order knowledge to discard unreachable nodes and greatly reduce the game tree considered.

That reduction carries a theoretical risk: the authors prove that their basic approach can increase exploitability relative to the original blueprint strategy. They establish safety through incorporating solved strategies back into the blueprint or restricting the information sets where solving occurs. Applying the method at every reached information set instead yields a weaker solution concept called affine equilibrium.

An affine equilibrium cannot be exploited by an opponent using a Nash strategy; exploiting it requires opening oneself to counter-exploitation. In experiments on medium-sized practical games, even the version without safety additions consistently reduced exploitability. A depth-limited version also produced what the authors describe, with a knowledge qualifier, as the first strong dark-chess AI. The paper therefore distinguishes practical improvements from the additional conditions needed for formal safety.
neurips-2021-subgame-solving-without-com.tldr: Using low-order knowledge makes hidden-information subgames smaller, with practical gains and specific conditions or weaker equilibrium guarantees for safety.

paragraphs: Tracking several people through video requires recognizing the same person despite changes in pose and viewpoint. This paper represents people through three-dimensional geometry, appearance, and location. Its Human Mesh and Appearance Recovery method extracts a SMPL body mesh and places appearance information on that mesh as a texture map.

Attaching appearance to the body’s surface provides a representation that is robust to changes in viewing angle and pose. For each detected person, the system extracts embeddings describing appearance, pose, and location. A transformer then combines these representations across space and time over the video sequence, allowing information from multiple observations to contribute to the tracking representation.

The system compares the resulting representations to associate detections with tracklets. Evaluations on Posetrack, MuPoTs, and AVA find the three-dimensional representations more effective than two-dimensional ones in these settings, with state-of-the-art tracking performance. The findings support using body-centered appearance together with geometry and temporal aggregation to maintain identity through visual changes, rather than relying solely on the appearance of an isolated two-dimensional detection.
neurips-2021-tracking-people-with-3d-rep.tldr: Combining textured 3D body representations with temporal aggregation improves multi-person tracking across the evaluated video datasets.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent learning often supplies a global reward even though individual agents need local value estimates. Value function factorization connects those two levels, but existing approaches commonly handle only a small number of agents. This paper hypothesizes that a flat factorization becomes a bottleneck as the team grows.

VAST introduces an intermediate level of variable sub-teams. It approximates factorization over these groups and then linearly decomposes each sub-team value among its members. Sub-teams can be defined arbitrarily and can change over time to suit different situations. This gives the original factorization operator a more compact and focused input representation.

The authors evaluate VAST in three multi-agent domains and find that it can significantly outperform state-of-the-art value factorization when the number of agents is sufficiently large. The qualification is central: the reported advantage concerns the scale where the proposed grouping addresses the suspected bottleneck. The contribution is a flexible organization of cooperative value learning, allowing group structure to change instead of forcing the same flat interaction among all agents throughout learning.
neurips-2021-vast-value-function-factori.tldr: VAST factors cooperative values through changing sub-teams and can improve performance when agent populations are sufficiently large.

paragraphs: Tabular prediction remains a setting where traditional methods such as gradient-boosted trees compete strongly with specialized neural networks. This paper asks whether plain multilayer perceptrons can perform better through a more careful combination of regularization methods. The central hypothesis is that jointly selecting those methods is an important part of neural-network performance.

For each dataset, the approach searches over a collection of 13 regularization techniques. It jointly decides which techniques to apply and how to set their associated hyperparameters. The resulting combination is dataset-specific, so the method treats regularization choices as interacting parts of a single optimization problem rather than independent fixed additions.

An empirical study across 40 tabular datasets finds that the resulting well-regularized multilayer perceptrons significantly outperform recent specialized neural architectures and also outperform strong traditional methods such as XGBoost. These findings establish the strength of the tested tuning approach on that collection of datasets. They also show why a simple network’s architecture alone is an incomplete description of its competitiveness: the jointly chosen training regularization can substantially affect the comparison.
neurips-2021-well-tuned-simple-nets-exce.tldr: Jointly tuning combinations of regularizers makes plain multilayer perceptrons outperform specialized neural models and strong tree methods in a 40-dataset study.
